lessons.title: ਇੱਕ, ਦੋ, ਤਿੰਨ, ਚਾਰ, ਪੰਜ — one to five
lessons.gloss: one to five — meeting the panj of Punjabi as an actual number

segments.text: Four of these are new. The fifth you have known since Chapter 5 — you just didn't know it was a number.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: the five

segments.text: This is Gurmukhi, not Devanagari — a related but distinct script. It does have a top line like Devanagari's, so words hang from a bar in the same way.
Two marks worth telling apart, because they look similar and do different jobs:
ੱ — the addak, on ikk. It doubles the following consonant.
ੰ — the tippi, on tinn and panj. It marks a nasal.
(So tinn's double n is not the addak's doing — that word is spelled with a nasal mark, and the doubling is in the pronunciation.)

blocks.title: What you've built: ਪੰਜ as a number

segments.text: Chapter 5 took the name ਪੰਜਾਬੀ (panjābī) apart for you: Persian ਪੰਜ panj, "five," plus ਆਬ āb, "water" — the language of the five rivers.
You learned panj there as a piece of a place-name. Here it arrives as what it actually is: the number five, an ordinary word you will count with.
The next prerequisite-ordered lesson explains an important twist: Punjabi's numeral and the Persian word reached the same panj shape independently.

segments.text: Count to five in Punjabi. (Ikk, do, tinn, chār, panj.) What script is this? (Gurmukhi — related to Devanagari, and it has a top line too.) What does ੱ and ੰ each do? (Addak doubles the following consonant; tippi marks a nasal.) Chapter 5 told you panjābī means "of the five rivers." What has changed now? (Panj is a number you can count with, not just a piece of a name.) Next: learn why Punjabi and Persian both say panj.

lessons.title: Why two branches both arrived at panj
lessons.gloss: why Punjabi and Persian independently reached the same word-shape for five

segments.text: Say “five” in Punjabi. (Panj.) Where did Chapter 5 first show that shape? (Inside Persian panj + āb, “five waters.”)

blocks.title: What you've built: the surprising family comparison

segments.text: The neighbours keep a -ch shape. Punjabi matches Persian -j, but the obvious borrowing story is wrong.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — Punjabi's numeral is homegrown

segments.text: Punjabi panj is inherited from Sanskrit pañca. North-western Indo-Aryan regularly voiced a stop after a nasal, turning -ñc- into -nj-.
Punjabi panjāh “fifty” (from Sanskrit pañcāśat) makes the rule visible; Hindi pacās shows the same source changing differently.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — Persian reached the shape separately

segments.text: Persian independently voiced ancestral č to j: Iranian panč became panj. Two Indo-Iranian branches therefore reached the same shape separately:

utterances: branch: Punjabi. path: Sanskrit pañca becomes nasal-triggered -nj-.
branch: Persian. path: Iranian panč becomes voiced panj.

segments.text: This is convergence, not borrowing. The place-name Punjab is Persian; Punjabi's look-alike numeral is inherited from Sanskrit.

segments.text: Borrowed from Persian? (No: Punjabi panj inherits Sanskrit pañca.) What made -nj-? (A post-nasal stop voiced.) Evidence? (Panjāh / pacās.) Persian's path? (Its ancestral č voiced separately.) In Punjab, what is Persian? (The place-name; Punjabi's number is homegrown.)

segments.prompt: Was Punjabi panj borrowed from Persian?

feedback.correct: Right: Punjabi panj inherits Sanskrit pañca; Persian reached a similar shape separately.
feedback.incorrect: No. Punjabi panj is inherited from Sanskrit pañca, not borrowed from Persian.
